summary: Gale Surface Ops is Team CheesySpace’s NASA Space Apps 2026 project: an offline mission planning and operations system for astronaut exploration at Mars’s Gale crater. It combines real terrain data, route planning, astronaut tablet and HUD views, and a habitat control console to track crew, supplies, communications, and hazards. Its demonstration replays a real solar radiation event, showing how local alerts and rover shelter coordination could help astronauts respond without waiting for Earth. Every displayed value identifies its source and whether it is measured, calculated, assumed, or simulated.
details:
Gale Surface Ops is an offline mission planning and surface operations prototype for human exploration at Gale crater, near Mount Sharp on Mars. Built by Team CheesySpace, it brings terrain maps, scientific destinations, astronaut navigation, habitat coordination, and emergency response into one shared system. Its central idea is that astronauts should be able to understand their surroundings and respond to hazards locally, even when communication with Earth is delayed.

The project supports the full journey of an extravehicular activity, or EVA: planning before departure, coordination during exploration, responding to changing conditions, and reviewing the mission afterward. It focuses on one detailed Exploration Zone rather than attempting to map the entire planet. This allows us to connect real terrain and scientific context to the practical decisions a crew would face on a surface excursion.

Before an EVA, users select exploration stops and build a route over real Gale crater imagery and elevation data. The planner combines a 25 cm HiRISE colour basemap, a 1 m merged terrain model, thermal-inertia information, and Curiosity’s recorded traverse. Users can inspect terrain, explore scientific points of interest, arrange waypoints, and evaluate a proposed mission.

The route engine searches for a least-time path across a terrain grid, taking account of slope limits and configured caution penalties. It produces route distances, elevation profiles, walking-time estimates, daylight information, and warnings. Habitat communication visibility and access to a safe haven help users assess the consequences of their choices. Walking speed, suit capacity, and vehicle characteristics are configurable model assumptions, so the interface makes their status visible.

Scientific stops connect navigation to exploration goals. The chosen area includes Mount Sharp’s boxwork formations, ridges, hollows, and sulfate-bearing terrain. Curiosity mission updates and locally stored photographs explain why these destinations matter and help users understand what the terrain looks like from the surface. Resource-related stops communicate the evidence behind an interpretation without presenting a prospecting target as a confirmed usable resource.

During the EVA, a local server called Hab Core maintains the mission’s shared simulation state. It coordinates the mission clock, simulated crew positions, consumable estimates, vehicles, task progress, communications, and alerts. Browser clients connect to it over the habitat’s local network.

Different interfaces serve different roles:

  • The habitat operations console gives the support crew a shared map, crew and vehicle information, task progress, alerts, and coordination controls.
  • The EVA tablet gives an astronaut navigation information, remaining resources, assigned tasks, and access to contingency actions.
  • The HUD view presents a small set of essential values for quick reading, including haven time, navigation, oxygen time remaining, alerts, and link status.
  • The mission report brings together task outcomes, timeline information, radiation exposure, and the event log for review.

These views share the same underlying state. An action taken through one role can be reflected in the others, demonstrating coordination between astronauts and habitat operators. The HUD is represented as a browser interface; the prototype does not require a physical helmet display.

The main demonstration replays the real solar particle event of 20 May 2024, sol 4190, using radiation measurements from Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector. Historical NASA DONKI records supply space-weather notification context, while SPICE-derived geometry represents Earth–Mars communication delay and orbital relay visibility.

As the recorded radiation rises, the habitat simulation detects the increase and issues an alert according to configured thresholds. The crew can evaluate contingency options, including requesting a pressurized rover rendezvous or returning to a haven. This makes the challenge of delayed Earth support visible: the habitat and surface crew need enough local information to act while distant communications are still in transit.

The scientific observations are real historical inputs, while astronauts, suits, rover movements, and operational responses are simulated. That distinction is central to the project. We use the historical event to explore an operational scenario rather than imply that the system is receiving live Mars telemetry.

The intended benefit is better shared understanding. A terrain map alone cannot explain whether a route fits within a crew’s available time, whether communication may be obstructed, or how a developing hazard changes the mission. Gale Surface Ops connects these questions in one environment. It is intended to help mission-concept designers, researchers, educators, and analog exploration teams examine the relationships between science objectives, terrain, resources, communications, and contingency planning.

The project also supports repeatable analysis. Its scientific calculations and simulation are deterministic: the same inputs and commands produce the same results. An event log records what happened, allowing a scenario to be replayed and reviewed. This helps users explain why an outcome occurred and compare operational choices.

We developed the system using:

Area

Tools and technologies

Web interfaces

TypeScript, React, HTML, CSS, and Vite

Mapping and coordinates

OpenLayers and Proj4js with a Mars-specific coordinate system

Habitat server

Node.js, Fastify, and WebSocket communication through ws

Scientific computation

A shared TypeScript computation package

Offline data processing

Python, GDAL, Rasterio, NumPy, and pyproj

Orbital and radiation processing

NASA SPICE through SpiceyPy, plus cdflib for radiation archive files

Validation and testing

JSON Schema, Ajv, Vitest, pytest, Playwright, and axe accessibility checks

Development assistance

Claude, Codex, Gemini, Puku CLI, and GitHub Copilot, documented in the project’s AI-use log

The deployment is designed around ordinary computing hardware: a laptop or local computer hosts Hab Core, and browser-capable devices connect over a local network. Map tiles, datasets, photographs, fonts, and icons are packaged locally. The application requires no internet connection or AI service at runtime.

Our creative contribution is the combination of a scientifically grounded map with a coordinated operational scenario. Users can move from choosing a science destination to following a route, handling tasks, experiencing a historical radiation event, coordinating shelter, and examining the resulting mission record. The real storm replay turns environmental data into an understandable sequence of decisions.

Throughout development, we considered communication delays, offline operation, terrain resolution, uncertainty, limited screen space, and the need to read critical information quickly. Alerts use words and shapes alongside colour. Interfaces prioritize essential information, provide visible source and provenance information, and indicate unavailable or stale values. Every displayed value identifies whether it is measured, derived, modelled, assumed, replayed, or simulated.

Gale Surface Ops is an exploratory prototype rather than certified astronaut operations software. Its intended impact is to demonstrate how transparent data, repeatable computation, and local coordination could support future Mars surface exploration—and to make those operational challenges accessible to people studying or designing such missions.
